label: Daniyel (Daniel) — Part 2 — Chapters 7–12
summary_plain: Daniyel chapters 7 through 12 contain the apocalyptic visions. Chapter 7: four great beasts rise from the sea — a lion, a bear, a leopard, and a terrifying fourth beast with iron teeth. The Ancient of Days takes his throne. One like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given dominion. Chapter 9: Daniyel prays and receives the vision of seventy weeks. Chapters 10-12: a final vision of wars between kings of the north and south, the time of trouble, and the resurrection — many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads Daniyel 7-12 from eight DSS manuscripts (4QDan-a through 4QDan-e, 1QDan-a, 1QDan-b, 6QDan) and the Orit Ge'ez. The 'one like a son of man' (ke-var enash) in 7:13 is critical. In the DSS framework and in the Aramaic original, this figure is collective and national — 'the saints of the Most High' who receive the kingdom (7:18, 7:27). The Aramaic bar enash means simply 'a human being, a mortal.' The figure is like a human being — in contrast to the four beasts who represent empires. The saints of the Most High are the covenant people, not a divine individual. The NT appropriation of 'Son of Man' as a divine title for an individual (Matthew 26:64, Mark 14:62) reverses the text's own interpretation: Daniyel 7:27 explicitly states 'the kingdom and the dominion shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High.' The kingdom is given to a people, not to a person. The DSS community at Qumran read this text as a national promise for the covenant community in the Period of Wrath.

key_terms.definition: Daniyel's vision of four great beasts rising from the sea: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear raised on one side with ribs in its mouth, a leopard with four wings and four heads, and a terrible fourth beast with iron teeth and ten horns — widely interpreted as representing successive world empires. The vision ends with the Ancient of Days seated in judgment and the dominion given to the Son of Man.

The figure in Daniyel 7:9-10 who presides over the heavenly court: seated on a throne with wheels of blazing fire, clothing like white snow, hair like pure wool, with ten thousand times ten thousand standing before him — a court of judgment in which the beasts are judged and their dominion taken away. The imagery is entirely within the Hebrew covenant tradition.

The figure in Daniyel 7:13-14 who comes 'with the clouds of heaven' to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples should serve — an everlasting dominion that will not pass away. 'Bar enash' is Aramaic for 'son of a human being' — a human figure in contrast to the beast-empires. The NT borrowed this language from Daniyel; Daniyel is the source, the NT derivative.

The vision given to Daniyel in ch.9 after his prayer responding to Yirmeyahu's seventy-year prophecy: seventy weeks of years (seventy times seven = 490 years) are decreed for the covenant people and the holy city; the vision outlines a framework of periods culminating in the anointing of a most holy place. The DSS community at Qumran read and interpreted this vision intensely.

Daniyel's vision in ch.8 of a two-horned ram (interpreted as Medo-Persia) and a goat with a conspicuous horn (interpreted as Greece/Alexander the Great) that destroys the ram; the goat's horn is broken and four horns arise; from one of them comes a 'little horn' that grows exceedingly great, casts down stars, removes the daily offering, and magnifies itself against the Prince of the host. The DSS community interpreted this as applying to Antiochus IV Epiphanes.

A figure appearing in both Daniyel 7:8 (rising among the ten horns of the fourth beast) and 8:9 (from one of the four horns of the broken goat); in ch.8 it destroys the daily offering and sets up an abomination; in ch.7 it speaks words against the Most High and wars against the holy ones; widely identified in context as Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164 BCE), who desecrated the Temple in 167 BCE.

The heavenly figure identified in Daniyel 10:21 and 12:1 as 'your prince' — the heavenly guardian of the covenant people; at the time of distress in 12:1, Mikhael stands up and 'your people shall be delivered, everyone whose name shall be found written in the book.' Mikhael is the first named angelic figure in the Hebrew scriptures with a specific protective role.

Daniyel 12:1 refers to 'the book' in which names are written, those who will be delivered at the time of distress: 'everyone whose name shall be found written in the book.' This is the clearest reference in the Hebrew scriptures to a heavenly record of the covenant community that determines who will be delivered. The concept appears throughout later covenant texts.

Daniyel 12:2 is one of the clearest statements of resurrection in the pre-Christian Hebrew corpus: 'Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.' This is not Greek immortality of the soul but physical awakening from the dust — consistent with the Hebrew Sheol-and-resurrection framework.

The phrase in Daniyel 9:27, 11:31, and 12:11 referring to the removal of the daily offering and the setting up of an abomination; in context, this describes Antiochus IV Epiphanes's desecration of the Temple in 167 BCE (1 Maccabees 1:54 uses the same phrase). The Qumran community used this language to frame their own period of persecution. The NT borrowed this phrase from Daniyel — Daniyel is the source.

faq.question: What is the significance of the four-beast vision in Daniyel 7?
faq.answer: The four beasts rising from the sea represent successive world empires that oppress the covenant people. The vision moves from empire to empire — each more terrible than the last — until the Ancient of Days convenes a heavenly court, the beasts are judged, and dominion is given to the Son of Man figure and to the people of the holy ones. The vision is a covenant declaration: human empires are temporary; YHWH's judgment is final; the covenant community will ultimately receive the kingdom.

faq.question: Who is the 'Son of Man' in Daniyel 7, and what is his significance?
faq.answer: The Son of Man ('bar enash' in Aramaic) is a human figure who receives eternal dominion from the Ancient of Days. In contrast to the beast-empires that rise from the sea, this human figure approaches from the clouds of heaven. The vision likely represents either a corporate symbol for the covenant people (the holy ones who inherit the kingdom, 7:27) or a heavenly figure representing them. The NT borrowed this language for the constructed figure — Daniyel 7 is the source; the NT is the derivative.

faq.question: What does Daniyel's prayer in ch.9 reveal about his theology?
faq.answer: Daniyel's prayer (9:4-19) is a covenant confession: he acknowledges the community's breach of the covenant, the justice of YHWH's punishment (the exile), and appeals not to any merit of the covenant people but entirely to YHWH's righteousness and mercy. 'We do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy' (9:18). This is the covenant structure of Devarim: breach, exile, confession, appeal, restoration.

faq.question: What does the seventy weeks prophecy in Daniyel 9 mean?
faq.answer: After Daniyel reads Yirmeyahu's seventy-year prophecy, the figure Gavri'el gives a vision of seventy 'weeks' of years (490 years) decreed for the covenant people. The vision outlines three periods: seven weeks, sixty-two weeks, and one final week — culminating in the anointing of a most holy place. The DSS Qumran community interpreted this framework as applying to their own period. The exact calculation has been read in many ways; the theological core is that YHWH has a determined timeline for the covenant people.

faq.question: How does Daniyel 12:2 fit into the Hebrew understanding of death and resurrection?
faq.answer: Daniyel 12:2 uses the language of sleeping in the dust — consistent with the Hebrew view of Sheol as the place of the dead, the dust of the earth. The resurrection described is a physical awakening from the dust, not the Greek immortality of the soul (which needs no resurrection because the soul never truly dies). This is the same framework as Yehezkel's valley of dry bones (ch.37) — the dead are truly dead, and their raising is an act of YHWH's power. Daniyel 12:2 is the clearest pre-Christian Hebrew resurrection statement.

faq.question: What is the role of Mikhael in Daniyel?
faq.answer: Mikhael appears in 10:13-21 as the heavenly prince of Yisra'el, engaged in conflict with the 'prince of Persia' and 'prince of Greece' — heavenly figures associated with empires. In 12:1 he stands up at the time of the greatest distress, and his standing is linked to the deliverance of those written in the book. Mikhael is the first named angelic figure in the Hebrew scriptures with a specific guardianship role over the covenant community. This divine-council framework is consistent with Devarim 32 and the Qumran corpus.

faq.question: What does Daniyel have to do with the Qumran community?
faq.answer: The Qumran Yahad community preserved at least eight copies of Daniyel and wrote multiple pesher (interpretive commentary) texts applying Daniyel's visions to their own period. They understood themselves as living in the final crisis period Daniyel described — the same seventy-week framework, the same abomination-era conflict. 4QFlorilegium and other Qumran texts cite Daniyel's Son of Man and the seventy weeks as a framework for the Teacher of Righteousness's era. Daniyel was a living operational text for the Qumran covenant community.

faq.question: What is the 'abomination of desolation' in Daniyel?
faq.answer: The phrase appears in 9:27, 11:31, and 12:11. In its historical context (Daniyel 11:31 especially), it refers to the actions of Antiochus IV Epiphanes in 167 BCE: removing the daily burnt offering and setting up an abomination in the Temple. 1 Maccabees 1:54 uses identical language. The Qumran community also applied this language to their own experience. The NT borrowed the phrase from Daniyel — the direction is from Daniyel forward, not from the NT backward.

faq.question: How does the book of Daniyel fit the Source Integrity rule?
faq.answer: Daniyel is a Second Temple period text physically composed c. 165 BCE, but it carries pre-Corruption First Temple covenant tradition: YHWH as the unsubstituted Name, the divine council (the Ancient of Days, the heavenly court, Mikhael), covenant accountability language (the prayer in ch.9), and the Hebrew resurrection framework (12:2 — dust and awakening, not Greek soul-immortality). It qualifies under Rule 25's pre-Corruption standard because the tradition it carries — not its physical composition date — is what determines its standing.

faq.question: What is the relationship between Daniyel's visions and 1 Enoch?
faq.answer: Both Daniyel and 1 Enoch (especially the Book of Watchers and the Similitudes) share the Ancient of Days imagery, the heavenly throne with wheels of fire, the angelic court, and the Son of Man figure. The Similitudes of Enoch develop the Son of Man language in ways that parallel and expand Daniyel 7. Both texts were central to the Qumran community. 1 Enoch's material predates or is contemporaneous with Daniyel; both draw on the same First Temple divine-council tradition. Neither text is derivative of NT — the NT borrowed from both.

faq.question: What does the vision of the ram and goat (Daniyel 8) reveal about the nature of these visions?
faq.answer: Daniyel 8 is unusual in that the angel Gavri'el explicitly names the figures being symbolized: the two-horned ram is Medo-Persia; the goat is Greece; the great horn is the first king (Alexander). This named interpretation establishes that the visions are not purely abstract — they refer to real historical empires and figures. The Qumran community and later readers used this interpretive framework to decode the more cryptic visions in chs 7 and 11-12.
